name: Cesta Tower
region: Mount Titano, City of San Marino, Republic of San Marino
address: Seconda Torre, Mount Titano, San Marino 47890
architectural_style: 13th-century medieval tower on the highest peak of Mount Titano; circular keep with crenellated parapet, connected by a curtain wall to the Montale (Third Tower); now houses the Museum of Ancient Weapons — approximately 700–2,000 pieces of arms and armour from the 15th to 20th centuries displayed within the tower's vaulted interior

opening_hours.seasonal_note: Open daily in season (April–October); hours reduced in winter. Entry is included in the State Museums Pass, which is bundled into the GYG guided tour (t1035756). The guided portion of the tour walks with a guide to Guaita Tower (First Tower); the State Museums Pass then allows self-paced access to Cesta Tower, the Museum of Ancient Weapons, and five additional sites.

visit_duration: 45–60 minutes at Cesta Tower; 3–4 hours total with the full 7-site State Museums Pass
accessibility: The path from San Marino City to Cesta Tower involves uphill walking along the ridge of Mount Titano — more demanding than the walk to Guaita Tower. The tower interior has spiral stairs. Not suitable for wheelchairs. The GYG guided tour covers Guaita first; Cesta is reached independently via the included pass.
tagline: San Marino's Second Tower on Mount Titano's highest peak — home to a 700-piece collection of medieval arms and armour, and one of seven sites covered by the State Museums Pass
highlights: The Museum of Ancient Weapons — Cesta Tower houses one of the most extensive collections of historical arms and armour in Italy and the surrounding region, with approximately 700 pieces ranging from 15th-century plate armour and crossbows through to 20th-century weapons; displayed within the tower's stone vaulted interior, with the medieval setting adding considerable atmosphere to the collection

San Marino's highest point — Cesta sits on the tallest of Mount Titano's three peaks at approximately 756m above sea level, giving panoramic views that extend to the Adriatic coast on clear days and across the Emilia-Romagna and Marche regions of Italy in every other direction

Part of the UNESCO-listed historic centre — the three towers of Mount Titano, including Cesta, are inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site (2008) along with the city's medieval urban fabric; the tower is the most historically significant component of the ridge's defensive system

The 7-site State Museums Pass — Cesta Tower is covered by the San Marino State Museums Pass, which also includes Palazzo Pubblico, Guaita Tower, Montale Tower (exterior), the State Museum, the Gallery of Modern and Contemporary Art, and the Museum of the Medieval Village; the GYG guided tour (t1035756) bundles this pass for all participants

The GYG small-group guided tour of San Marino (t1035756, from €45, 4.9★ / 31 reviews) includes the State Museums Pass as part of the tour price; a guide leads the group to Guaita Tower, then participants use the pass self-paced for Cesta and the remaining sites
description:
Cesta Tower stands on the highest of Mount Titano's three rocky peaks — the summit that gives it not only strategic dominance over the ridge but also the most dramatic views in San Marino. Its name is thought to derive from the Latin 'cista' (basket or container), possibly referring to the tower's role as a stronghold for arms and materials, a function it still performs in a museum context: the interior now houses the Museum of Ancient Weapons, with a collection of approximately 700 pieces spanning five centuries of European arms and armour.

The collection was assembled by San Marino and spans the period from the 15th to the 20th century — crossbows and plate armour from the late medieval period, swords, halberds, and firearms from the early modern era, and later military equipment through to the 20th century. The museum's setting within the tower's stone vaulted interior adds a contextual weight that a conventional museum gallery cannot replicate: these are arms being displayed in the building type for which they were originally designed.

Cesta is the second of San Marino's three towers, all of which sit on the Titano ridge and are connected by walkways and walls. Guaita (the First Tower, 11th century) is the most photographed and the most-visited; Montale (the Third Tower, 14th century) is accessible only from the exterior. Cesta occupies the intermediate position both chronologically and geographically, its 13th-century construction filling the ridge's defensive sequence. All three towers, along with the medieval historic centre below, are inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site (2008).

The GYG small-group guided tour (t1035756) is the most efficient way to access the full range of San Marino's heritage sites. The tour includes a professional guide who leads the group along the ridge path to Guaita Tower, explaining the republic's improbable political history — Europe's smallest state and (by San Marino's own account) the world's oldest surviving republic. At Guaita, the guided portion of the tour ends. Participants then receive the State Museums Pass, which grants access to Cesta Tower and the Museum of Ancient Weapons, Palazzo Pubblico (when open), Montale Tower's exterior, the State Museum, the Gallery of Modern and Contemporary Art, and the Museum of the Medieval Village. The pass allows self-paced visiting of all remaining sites, with no time constraint imposed by the tour structure. Cesta Tower is confirmed by name in both the tour's Full Description and the Includes list as one of the seven covered sites.
history: The three towers of Mount Titano are documented from different periods: Guaita (First Tower) from the 11th century, Cesta (Second Tower) from 1253, and Montale (Third Tower) from approximately 1353. Cesta's 13th-century construction extended the defensive coverage of the Titano ridge toward its highest point, completing the essential structure of San Marino's mountain fortification system. The tower was used militarily through the medieval and early modern periods and at various points served as a prison. The arms collection now housed in the Museum of Ancient Weapons was assembled in the 20th century and installed in the tower in its current museum form. San Marino's historic centre and Mount Titano were inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2008, with the three towers as the primary natural and architectural components of the inscription.
how_to_visit:
**Getting there:** San Marino City is accessible from Rimini by bus (Bonelli bus line, approximately 45 minutes from Rimini railway station, running several times daily). By car from Rimini, take the SP258 toward San Marino (~30 minutes). Cesta Tower is reached from the city centre via the ridge path — a 20–30 minute walk from the main Piazza della Libertà, uphill along the fortification walkway beyond Guaita Tower.

**Tickets:** Walk-up access to Cesta Tower and the Museum of Ancient Weapons is covered by the State Museums Pass (approximately €5 per adult). The GYG small-group guided tour of San Marino (t1035756, from €45 per person, 4.9★ / 31 reviews) includes the State Museums Pass for all 7 sites. The guided portion walks to Guaita Tower with the group; Cesta and the remaining 5 sites are then explored self-paced with the included pass.

**Practical tips:** Allow at least 45 minutes at Cesta Tower for the Museum of Ancient Weapons; the collection is larger than visitors typically expect. The ridge walk between Guaita and Cesta takes about 15 minutes and involves some climbing on stone paths. The highest point of the Cesta parapet gives the widest view in San Marino — the Adriatic is visible on a clear day. Combine with Guaita Tower (already visible from the ridge path) and Palazzo Pubblico in the city centre for the most complete circuit.

**Combine with:** [Guaita Tower](/castles/san-marino/guaita-tower) (San Marino's iconic First Tower on the ridge — the most-photographed medieval structure in the republic, reached first on the GYG guided walk, with views over the city and the Emilia-Romagna plain) and [Palazzo Pubblico](/castles/san-marino/palazzo-pubblico) (the neo-Gothic seat of the Captains Regent in Piazza della Libertà — also covered by the same State Museums Pass, with the ceremonial changing of the guard in full medieval costume).

faqs.question: How does the GYG tour structure work — is the whole tour guided, or just part of it?
faqs.answer: The GYG guided tour (t1035756) is structured in two phases. The first phase is a guided small-group walk: a professional guide leads participants from the city centre along the ridge path to Guaita Tower, explaining San Marino's history, the tower system, and the republic's political structure along the way. This guided phase typically lasts 1–1.5 hours. At Guaita Tower, the guided portion ends and participants receive the State Museums Pass. The second phase is self-paced: with the pass, participants can visit Cesta Tower and its Museum of Ancient Weapons, Palazzo Pubblico (when open), Montale Tower (exterior), the State Museum, the Gallery of Modern and Contemporary Art, and the Museum of the Medieval Village, in any order and at any pace. Total time for the full 7-site programme is typically 3–4 hours.

faqs.question: What period does the Museum of Ancient Weapons collection cover, and how significant is it?
faqs.answer: The Museum of Ancient Weapons holds approximately 700 pieces spanning the 15th to 20th centuries — crossbows and plate armour from the late medieval period, early modern firearms, swords, halberds, pistols, and later military equipment through the 20th century. The collection's significance lies partly in its scope and partly in its location: relatively few medieval tower interiors in Europe display an arms collection this extensive within the original defensive architecture. The breadth of period covered means the museum tells a coherent story of arms development over five centuries rather than focusing on a single era.

faqs.question: Can visitors do just Cesta Tower without the full guided tour?
faqs.answer: Yes — the State Museums Pass can be purchased independently at any of the covered sites, including Cesta Tower, for approximately €5 per adult. Walk-up visitors buy the pass at the entrance and proceed directly. The GYG guided tour (t1035756) bundles the same pass with a professional guided walk to Guaita Tower at the start; visitors who want expert context on San Marino's history before exploring independently will find the guided format worth the additional cost, particularly for the ridge walk and Guaita section.
